findings.body: Any request `Origin` is now copied into `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` while `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` is always `true`. A page at an attacker origin can send the victim's cookies/credentials to this API and read the response; the previous allowlist (`https://app.example.com`) blocked that. Native mobile clients do not enforce CORS, and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials is invalid in browsers, so this also fails the no-origin path it claims to fix. Keep an explicit allowlist (add known webview origins if needed) and omit CORS headers when `origin` is null or not listed.

summary:
This change turns a single-origin allowlist into a credentialed CORS reflector: any `Origin` is echoed back with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. That lets any website read authenticated API responses in the victim's browser.

The stated mobile-client goal does not require this. Native HTTP stacks do not enforce CORS. Browser webviews that do send an origin belong on a finite allowlist (`https://app.example.com`, `capacitor://localhost`, and similar known schemes). When `origin` is null, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` plus credentials is also invalid per the Fetch CORS spec, so browsers reject the response.

`Vary: Origin` is the right cache header for origin-specific ACAO, but it does not mitigate reflecting untrusted origins.

**Recommendation:** request-changes
